new_statements.rule_in_words: One primary stress per phonological word, on the lexical root: native words are CV́TV or TV́ with the stressed syllable preceding the medial (voiceless, often geminate) obstruent, i.e. a trochaic foot on the root; proclitics and enclitics are unstressed ([[proclitic [stressed root]] enclitic] per Bueno Holle 2019: 18 reporting Sicoli 2007). Word-final stress is foreign to the native system and survives only in unassimilated Spanish loans. In a bare disyllabic root this is penultimate stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Sicoli 1999 is silent. Bueno Holle 2019: 18, reporting Sicoli 2007: 'only primary (no secondary) stress which is non-iterative, that is, has at most one stress foot'.
new_statements.exceptions: Unassimilated Spanish loans may keep final-syllable stress (kolcho!n [kolˈtʃoŋ] 'mattress', jardin [xarˈdin] 'garden'); 'Stress on some loanwords may not follow from otherwise predictable rules' (p. 396). Assimilated loans take the native pattern (kalo [ˈkal:o] 'broth', sonaja [soˈnax:a] 'rattle').
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (root plus clitics); the 1999 examples are isolated citation forms in a practical orthography with an acute accent marking stress and IPA with ˈ. The statement is indirect: Sicoli states that native words have a stressed syllable before the medial obstruent (CVTV) and that final stress violates native constraints; he never writes a one-line stress rule. Phrase-level emphasis (gemination/lengthening of the stressed foot) and boundary tones are described in Sicoli 2007 per Bueno Holle 2019: 18.
new_statements.identity_note: All opened sources describe the Zapotec of Santa María Lachixío (Sola de Vega district, Oaxaca), which Sicoli 1999: 395 calls 'a dialect of the Solteco branch'; this is Glottolog lach1249 / ISO zpl (also listed under Zimatlán/Western Zapotec names). Sicoli 2007 additionally covers Asunción Mixtepec Zapotec (zoo, asun1236); the Bueno Holle 2019 report concerns Lachixío only.

new_statements.quote: [p. 396] Stress on some loanwords may not follow from otherwise predictable rules. These words show high transfer of phonological patterns from the source language. Example (3) shows the preservation of a liquid-obstruent sequence, a syllable (and word) final nasal, and final syllable stress. All of these features violate the system of phonological constraints that were operational in the precontact Lachixio phonological system. new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record has an empty rule; the existing_statement is this same paper (same p. 396 quote) but labelled 'morphologically determined', which the text does not support: Sicoli says native stress is rule-predictable and non-final and says nothing about morphological conditioning. The 1999 evidence is compatible with the second-hand report of Sicoli 2007 in Bueno Holle 2019 (one primary stress per phonological word on the root, trochaic foot, no secondary stress).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress in native Lachixío words follows predictable rules and is not word-final: final-syllable stress (as in the unassimilated loan kolchón 'mattress', p. 396) is one of the features that violate the precontact system, while the assimilated loan kalo ['kal:o] < caldo (p. 395) carries stress on the first syllable, and native disyllables are described as CVTV with the medial obstruent 'after a stressed syllable', i.e. stress on the first (penultimate) syllable of a CVCV word. The paper never states the rule outright; 'penultimate/root-initial, non-final, predictable' is an inference from these three passages.
new_statements.exceptions: Unassimilated Spanish loanwords may keep final-syllable stress and other foreign features (p. 396); stress on such loans 'may not follow from otherwise predictable rules'.
new_statements.identity_note: Persons 1997 describes Santa María Lachixío (district of Sola de Vega, Oaxaca) and names San Vicente Lachixío and San Miguel Mixtepec as closely related varieties (about 85% intelligibility); Sicoli 1999 writes simply 'Lachixío' (his field site is Santa María Lachixío in the 2007/2010 work). Nothing opened describes a different variety.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement between the sources themselves. Sicoli 1999 (first-hand): native stress is predictable and non-final, first syllable of CVCV native words stressed, Spanish loans may keep final stress. Bueno Holle 2019 (held by the project, second-hand summary of Sicoli 2007 pp. 18-19): Lachixío has 'only primary (no secondary) stress which is non-iterative', a trochaic foot, and a maximal phonological word [[proclitic [stressed root]] enclitic]. Sicoli 2010 (held by the project) adds phonemic low tone (imperative marked by L) and says nothing about stress placement; Persons 1997 describes a high-pitch respect register only. The one conflict is with the catalog's own label: the existing statement tags Sicoli 1999 as 'morphologically determined', a reading the text does not contain.

sources.note: Second-hand report of Sicoli 2007: 'He describes Lachixío Zapotec as a "stress-timed" language where there is only primary (no secondary) stress which is non-iterative, that is, has at most one stress foot.. The maximal phonological word is composed of a clitic phrase with the following structure: [[proclitic [stressed root]] enclitic]. The metrical foot, the unit counted for rhythm, is trochaic.' Emphasis marked by geminate medial consonant or lengthened stressed vowel of the primary foot (p. 18).
